WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- When shots rang out at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum last week, security officers Harry Weeks and Jason McCuiston were stunned. Harry Weeks, left, and Jason McCuiston fired on James von Brunn at the Holocaust Memorial Museum. "I would say it was surreal, both of us couldn't believe what was happening," Weeks told CNN in his first national televised interview since the June 10 shooting. "I know myself I just, I heard 'pop, pop' and it was surreal." McCuiston added: "It wasn't normal. You knew something was wrong and you knew it was very bad." What went terribly wrong is that white supremacist James von Brunn allegedly walked into the museum and started firing his rifle, shooting security officer Stephen Johns in the chest. Despite their initial shock, Weeks and McCuiston kept their composure enough to draw their weapons and start shooting at von Brunn, 88. Weeks had fired his gun in the line of duty 25 years earlier as a Washington, D.C., police officer. But he said nothing compared to this bloody confrontation. "This was terrible," Weeks said softly. "This was worse. ... We lost Officer Johns." Johns died shortly after the shooting, leaving behind a family that includes a teenage son who told CNN affiliate WUSA-TV the day after the tragedy that his dad was "my hero." Watching a video clip of those comments, McCuiston started crying. "First thing I thought about, I have an 11-year-old," the officer said before breaking down.  Watch the officers tell their story » . Just moments before their joint interview with CNN on Thursday, McCuiston and Weeks attended a grief counseling session together, and both men say they are still struggling with their emotions. The security officers said they believe von Brunn will survive his wounds and eventually face trial. So they would not discuss details of the shootout out of a fear of jeopardizing the criminal investigation, but they were willing to discuss their memories of Johns so that the public knows more about him. McCuiston said the 6-foot-6-inch, 300-pound Johns was a "gentle giant" who was always friendly to colleagues and museum visitors. "Just an awesome guy," he recalled. "Grin from ear to ear. You'd never know that man probably ever had a bad day in his life." Weeks said he wanted the world to see "what a man of hate did to this family, and the grief he caused. Let's all remember Officer Johns, and his family, because he took the ultimate -- he did his job and he was where he was supposed to be -- and the family suffered. That could have been anyone." McCuiston and Weeks, however, deflected suggestions that they may be heroes as well because if they had not stopped von Brunn, there's no telling how many of the more than 2,000 people visiting the museum at the time could have been injured or killed. "A lot of people are going to be saying what they have been saying, 'You are a hero, you're this, you're that,' " McCuiston said. "It's like we tell everybody, 'We chose this job, it's a job. It's the same as a firefighter who would walk into a building, that is his job, he chose to do it.' " Johns' funeral on Friday has been moved to a larger church in the Washington area to accommodate all of the people who want to attend, and the museum will be closed most of the day so that his colleagues can attend. "Everyone knows when you lose someone, death is one of the worst things, even though it is reality," McCuiston said. "Time will hopefully heal all, and hopefully there will be a little bit of closure with us and the family and we can all just move forward but never forget what a wonderful man he was."

outputs.L1:
**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** When shots rang out at the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum last week, security officers Harry Weeks and Jason McCuiston were stunned.

Weeks, left, and McCuiston opened fire on James von Brunn at the Holocaust Memorial Museum.

“I would say it was surreal. Neither of us could believe what was happening,” Weeks told CNN in his first nationally televised interview since the June 10 shooting. “I know that I just heard ‘pop, pop,’ and it was surreal.”

McCuiston added, “It wasn’t normal. You knew something was wrong, and you knew it was very bad.”

What went terribly wrong, authorities allege, was that white supremacist James von Brunn entered the museum and began firing his rifle, shooting security officer Stephen Johns in the chest.

Despite their initial shock, Weeks and McCuiston maintained enough composure to draw their weapons and return fire at von Brunn, 88.

Weeks had fired his gun in the line of duty 25 years earlier while serving as a Washington, D.C., police officer. But, he said, nothing compared with this bloody confrontation.

“This was terrible,” Weeks said softly. “This was worse. … We lost Officer Johns.”

Johns died shortly after the shooting, leaving behind a family that includes a teenage son. The day after the tragedy, his son told CNN affiliate WUSA-TV that his father was “my hero.”

As he watched a video clip of those remarks, McCuiston began to cry.

“The first thing I thought about was that I have an 11-year-old,” the officer said before breaking down.

*Watch the officers tell their story.*

Just moments before their joint interview with CNN on Thursday, McCuiston and Weeks attended a grief-counseling session together. Both men said they were still struggling with their emotions.

The security officers said they believed von Brunn would survive his wounds and eventually face trial. Out of concern that they might jeopardize the criminal investigation, they declined to discuss details of the shootout. They were, however, willing to share their memories of Johns so the public could learn more about him.

McCuiston described the 6-foot-6-inch, 300-pound Johns as a “gentle giant” who was always friendly to colleagues and museum visitors.

“Just an awesome guy,” he recalled. “Grin from ear to ear. You’d never know that man probably ever had a bad day in his life.”

Weeks said he wanted the world to see “what a man of hate did to this family and the grief he caused.”

“Let’s all remember Officer Johns and his family, because he made the ultimate sacrifice—he did his job, and he was where he was supposed to be—and the family suffered,” Weeks said. “That could have been anyone.”

McCuiston and Weeks, however, rejected suggestions that they, too, might be heroes. Had they not stopped von Brunn, there is no telling how many of the more than 2,000 people visiting the museum at the time might have been injured or killed.

“A lot of people are going to keep saying what they have been saying: ‘You are a hero; you’re this; you’re that,’” McCuiston said. “It’s like we tell everybody: ‘We chose this job. It’s a job. It’s the same as a firefighter who walks into a building—that is his job; he chose to do it.’”

Johns’ funeral on Friday was moved to a larger church in the Washington area to accommodate everyone wishing to attend. The museum will be closed for most of the day so his colleagues can be present.

“Everyone knows that when you lose someone, death is one of the worst things, even though it is a reality,” McCuiston said. “Time will hopefully heal all, and hopefully there will be a little bit of closure for us and the family. We can all move forward, but never forget what a wonderful man he was.”

In their first nationally televised interview since the shooting, Weeks told CNN that the experience felt unreal. After hearing two popping sounds, he said, neither officer could initially believe what was unfolding.

McCuiston said the situation was clearly abnormal and that they immediately understood something was seriously wrong.

Authorities allege that von Brunn, an 88-year-old white supremacist, entered the museum carrying a rifle and opened fire, striking security officer Stephen Johns in the chest. Although Weeks and McCuiston were initially stunned, they remained calm enough to pull their weapons and shoot at von Brunn.

Weeks had previously discharged his weapon while serving as a Washington, D.C., police officer 25 years earlier. Still, he said that incident did not compare with the violence at the museum. Speaking quietly, Weeks described the confrontation as far worse because Officer Johns was killed.

Johns died soon after the attack. He left behind a family that includes a teenage son, who told CNN affiliate WUSA-TV the following day that his father was his hero.

McCuiston began to cry while watching footage of the teenager’s remarks. Before becoming too emotional to continue, he said his first thought was of his own 11-year-old child.

Shortly before speaking jointly with CNN on Thursday, Weeks and McCuiston attended a grief-counseling session together. Both acknowledged that they were continuing to wrestle with their emotions.

The officers said they expected von Brunn to recover from his injuries and ultimately stand trial. Concerned that their comments might interfere with the criminal investigation, they declined to provide details about the exchange of gunfire. They were, however, willing to share memories of Johns so the public could learn more about him.

McCuiston described Johns, who stood 6 feet 6 inches tall and weighed 300 pounds, as a “gentle giant.” He said Johns was consistently kind to both coworkers and museum guests, calling him an extraordinary person who always wore a broad smile and never seemed to have a bad day.

Weeks said he wanted people to understand what one hateful individual had done to Johns’ family and how much sorrow he had caused. He urged the public to remember Johns and his loved ones, noting that the officer made the ultimate sacrifice while doing exactly what his job required. Weeks added that the victim could have been anyone.

McCuiston and Weeks rejected the idea that they should also be considered heroes, even though stopping von Brunn may have prevented additional casualties among the more than 2,000 visitors inside the museum at the time.

McCuiston said people would continue praising them as heroes, but he emphasized that they had voluntarily chosen security work and were simply performing their duties. He compared their actions to those of a firefighter entering a burning building because that is the profession the firefighter chose.

Johns’ funeral, scheduled for Friday, was relocated to a larger church in the Washington area to make room for the many expected mourners. The museum also planned to remain closed for most of the day, allowing his colleagues to attend the service.

McCuiston said losing someone is among life’s most painful experiences, despite death being unavoidable. He expressed hope that time would bring healing and some measure of closure to the officers and Johns’ family, enabling them to move ahead without ever forgetting what a remarkable man Johns had been.
